Death with Dignity

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...should you have the right to decide on your own death?

Unique Selling Point:
In the news: Sean Davison being arrested and accused of murder for helping a friend to die.

Summary:
Prof Sean Davison of Dignity SA was on 18 September arrested for murder for helping a friend, to die. In this insert we explore the issue, the legalities and talk to the main role players in the whole issue around assisted dying.

Further information:
The founder of right-to-die organisation, DignitySA, Sean Davison, has been arrested on a murder charge in Cape Town, a colleague and co-founder confirmed on Wednesday.

Davison was arrested on Tuesday, apparently over the death of his friend Anrich Burger in 2013. Burger became a quadriplegic after a car crash.Davison, the professor who helped his mother commit suicide in New Zealand, revealed to News24 in 2014 that he helped Burger end his life. DignitySA co-founder Willem Landman said police executed a search warrant and confiscated Davison's cellphone and laptop.He was kept in Sea Point police station overnight and was due to appear in Cape Town Magistrate's Court on Wednesday.


Landman understood that the State wanted R100 000 bail but an amount of R20 000 bail was settled on, which still had to be accepted by a magistrate. Western Cape police spokesperson Lieutenant-Colonel Andre Traut confirmed to News24 that an arrest was made relating to the 2013 death. "This office can confirm that a 57-year-old man was arrested on a charge of murder yesterday relating to an incident in Sea Point on November 2‚ 2013‚ which led to the death of a 43-year-old man. "The suspect is due to make a court appearance in Cape Town today [Wednesday] to face the charge against him."Founder of right-to-die organisation DignitySA, Sean Davison, maintains he has not committed an offence, after making his first appearance in the Cape Town Magistrate's Court on Wednesday for allegedly killing his friend, Anrich Burger. "It is and has always been my contention that I have not committed any offence as alleged in this matter," his lawyer Joshua Greeff read from an affidavit. Davison, 57, was arrested at his home in Pinelands on Tuesday for the 2013 death of Burger, who became a quadriplegic after a car crash. Davison, the professor who helped his mother end her life in New Zealand, revealed to News24 in 2014 that he helped Burger to do the same. Police conducted a search and seizure at his home this week. DignitySA co-founder Willem Landman told News24 Davison's phone and laptop were also confiscated. Prosecutor Megan Blows said the State alleged that the murder was planned or premeditated. She also said "new information has come to light... the accused might have committed other similar offences". It was not immediately clear to which other deaths she was referring. Davison's affidavit in support of his release on bail highlighted an extensive academic career and memberships to numerous professional organisations. He has been a professor of biotechnology at the University of the Western Cape since 2004 and heads up the forensic DNA laboratory there. He helped the Truth and Reconciliation Commission identify the remains of anti-apartheid activists, including the Mamelodi 10 of Pretoria. He also developed a DNA kit to help identify suspects in gang rapes, a service that was offered free to rape victims. In arguing to be released on bail, Davison said he had built an "impeccable reputation" over the years and incarceration could destroy his character and all for which he had worked. He said his three children would not understand his absence because he was an integral part of their lives. As the breadwinner for their family, Davison also feared his wife would not cope financially and emotionally. The court heard that being in custody would jeopardise several projects, outstanding DNA analysis and students under supervision, who Davison assisted. The investigating officer was in possession of his South African and New Zealand passports.

Davison pointed out that he abided by all bail conditions while standing trial in New Zealand for helping his cancer-stricken mother end her life. At the time, he pleaded guilty to assisted suicide in the Dunedin High Court and was sentenced to five months' house arrest. He was granted R20 000 bail on Wednesday, which included conditions, such as only leaving the Western Cape with the police's consent and reporting to a police station once a week. On the allegations, Landman said: "The organisation is on record that we stand for changing the law in South Africa to conform with the Constitution and... we do not assist people to die." "What anyone does in their private capacity is their own matter." Davison's arrest has put euthanasia back in the spotlight. In 2015, the North Gauteng High Court in Pretoria ruled that terminally-ill Cape Town advocate Robin Stransham-Ford, 65, had the right to commit suicide with a doctor's help. The following year, the Supreme Court of Appeal found it was wrong for the High Court to issue the order and that it did not fully consider the principles and ambit of changing the common law to encompass consent as a defence to a charge of murder. Stransham-Ford died two hours before the order was granted, as a result of his cancer.

Weighing in on Davison's case, defence lawyer William Booth said there had been a number of serious debates in the last decade to change the law on assisted suicide or voluntary euthanasia. "In my opinion, it should be legal under certain circumstances. No legislation has been promulgated where strict criteria is in place," he said. "This is about human dignity. If somebody is going to die... alleviate pain and suffering not only for the patient, but the family too." Davison said in 2012 that many doctors had told him in private that they had helped people to die at their request. "If you don't have a law change, you might be playing Lotto with your doctor." Davison is expected to be back in court on November 16.

Since then Archhbishop Emeritus Desmond Tutu has also come out in support of Davison.

Treatment:
1. We will follow up on our story of Robin Stransham-Ford who died just before his application to have assisted dying was granted. the ruling was overturned by SCA, but since then two more cases and requests have been lodged. We will speak to his wife and daughter -- Penelope and Epiphany.

2. We will speak to the mother of the person Davison helped to die, and get her perspective -- Wilma Du Pisani

3. In addition we have an exclusive interview with Sean Davison about his mother and how he helped her. We will try and get hold of him, although he has been advised not to speak to the media.

4. We will also speak to Willem Landman, co-founder of Dignity SA.

5. Dr Albertus van Eeden heads up Doctors for Life who are against this.

6. We have also secured an interview with Sally Buitendag, Dognity SA's lawyer. She also represented Stransham-Ford and will represent Davison now. She can speak about all the legal aspects.

Press Release:


Death with Dignity
Arrested, detained and out on R20,000 bail on a charge of murder, Prof. Sean Davison faces the fight of his life after helping his friend – in 2013 – to end a life of suffering after he’d become a paraplegic in a car crash. Meanwhile two more people have applied to the High Court for the right to die at a time they choose – an act that remains illegal in South Africa. Carte Blanche examines the complex and painful decisions around fighting for the right to die.
Producer: Eugene Botha
Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


Dieter Harck:
Throughout my life I have enjoyed physical activity…
V/O:
Dieter Harck suffers from Motor Neuron Disease and gets emotional when he thinks of how much the disease has stolen from him. He used to be a property company director and has adult children and several grandchildren. His partner of 18 years, Lynne Grubb, remembers his endless energy.
Lynne:
He was extremely active. He was either on his cycle doing a 100 km’s every morning, or at the gym.
V/O:
But the illness that was diagnosed in 2013 changed all that.
Lynne:
Dieter is unable to do anything at all for himself. He cannot carry a cup of coffee to his desk. Life for Dieter Harck is a battle. Every day is a battle.
V/O:
And Dieter knows that in time he will become completely paralysed, and slowly suffocate to death.
Dieter:
Friends we got to know died, certainly not a death I would wish on anybody.
LINK:
Dieter has now made the decision that when things become unbearable for him, he wants to end his life with the help of a physician, before the suffering gets too much.
V/O:
He, together with another terminally ill individual, a Dr Sue Walters who is dying from cancer, have recently launched an action in the Gauteng North High Court to have Assisted Dying legalized.

Prof. Willem Landman of Stellenbosch is the co- founder, or an NGO called Dignity South Africa and says there are two kinds of assisted dying.
Willem:
The one is called physician assisted suicide. A provides the means to B, who self-administers and dies. Physician assisted euthanasia is A supplies and administers to B who the dies as a consequence.
3. LINK:
Harck and Dr Walters want to change the law because assisted dying in South Africa is considered illegal and for anybody participating can lead to arrest and a charge of murder.
V/O:
This is exactly what has happened to Prof Sean Davison of Cape Town, the co-founder of Dignity South Africa. Here he is opening a world conference on assisted dying in Cape Town in September this year. A week after the conference he was arrested and charged with the murder of a very close friend of his, Dr Anrich Burger.

Burger once was a medical doctor and very active. In 2005 he was in a car accident in Bostwana, broke his neck and was completely paralysed.
Clip: Davison
But for Dr Burger, in addition to the undignified life, his body was racked with pain. Now Dr Burger was a medical doctor, he knew all the remedies available to relieve pain. He had tried them all and nothing had worked. For Dr Burger life was miserable. He was desperate to die.
V/O:
In 2013 he asked Davison to help him to die in a hotel at the Cape Town Waterfront
Clip: Davison
He asked me to be involved in his death, but he planned it. He was a medical doctor and he wrote the prescription for the medication to end his life. He arranged for a care-giver to take him to the pharmacy to collect the medication. He booked a hotel room at the Waterfront. At the end he wanted me to be there as a friend. Dr Burger committed suicide.
V/O:
That was 5 years ago, then out of the blue, on the 18 of September Davison, was arrested on a charge of murder and later released on bail.
4. LINK:
We asked the NPA why now, after five years, has he been arrested. They sent us a press release, Davison’s affidavit and highlighted the following:

“This is not an ordinary murder case and toxicology results are normally a lengthy process. The accused was also not in SA for a period of time. The SAPS was informed that the accused would be entering the RSA hence the arrest.”

They also said that “new information obtained suggests that the accused may have committed murder in a similar fashion on more than one occasion”.
V/O:
Davison is due back in court in November.

However, this is not his first brush with the law – in 2010 he was arrested in New Zealand for helping his mother who lived there, to die. He described it in a book and later served 5 months in house arrest after pleading guilty to a charge of assisted suicide.

In 2012 he co-founded Dignity South Africa together with Prof Willem Landman.
Willem:
We founded the NGO with a focus on changing the law. That was our aim. It is still our aim to change the law in South Africa so that people who suffer in a terminal stage of suffering that they can be legitimately and lawfully assisted by qualified people to die in a way that takes away their suffering.
V/O:
Sheena Swemmer of the Centre for Applied Legal Studies at Wits supports the legal action by Dieter and Dr Sue Walters. She links assisted dying to human rights.
Sheena:
To be refused the right to choose when to die when in these terminal circumstances is an infringement of one’s right to dignity, one’s right to equality, which together forms the right to autonomy as an individual. Dignified death is part of your right to life.
V/O:
The current action in the High Court to legalize assisted dying, is not the first of its kind in South Africa. In 2015 terminally ill advocate Robin Stransham-Ford petitioned the Gauteng North High Court to have the right to choose the time and manner of his death.
Sheena:
So various State Departments opposed the application and it was heard in court, in urgent court. It was presented on the papers, and when we say it was presented on the papers in legal terminology, what we mean is that it is prepared, the entire case is set out on paper, and the judge will decide on that. The judge will not hear any evidence, spoken evidence from experts.
V/O:
In a landmark ruling Judge Hans Frabricius found in favour of Stransham-Ford, and granted the application. However, the court victory came too late, says Epiphany Stransham-Ford, his daughter.
Epihany:
It was very bitter-sweet because he had died at 8 o’clock in the morning and the ruling had been passed down only two hours after that.
V/O:
Epiphany has never questioned or resented her father’s wish to end his life.. He really suffered.
Epiphany:
Towards the end of his life he could not move, he could not swallow, he could not blink. He was breathing, and his heart was beating but he was not living a life that was worth living. It was his death and I believe he should have been allowed to choose how his end should have come.
LINK:
Shortly after, various State departments that opposed the Stansham-Ford application, appealed the ruling by the High Court.
V/O:
The appeal was based on the fact that Stransham-Ford had died before the judgement was handed down and also because in the High Court case there was no thorough interrogation of witnesses because it was an urgent on the papers application.

So, the Appeal’s Court rescinded the judgment that assisted dying was legal, based on the technical reasons. However, the Court indicated that it was not unsympathetic towards the merits of the case.
Reginald:
The Supreme Court of Appeal left a door open for a case to be taken to the High Court again with all the evidence and all the facts.
V/O:
Reginald Tshabalala is Dieter Harcks’ attorney in the new case and this time round there will a thorough examination of all the evidence through expert witnesses.
Derek:
The Stransham-Ford case was severely affected when he died. What will happen in either of your clients die?
Reginald:
The nature of the action that we’ve instituted is so that the action will continue even though they may die in the meantime.
V/O:
A number of State Departments are opposing the action. This includes the Health professionals Council. Dr Kgosi Letlape is the President of the HPCSA.
Letlape:
Assisted dying in all is forms, whether it is active or passive, is unlawful in South Africa. It is also unprofessional conduct in terms of our code of ethics. So it is not permissible in the Republic of South Africa. We support proper palliative care, we are in negotiation and the Ministry is leading a path to ensure that palliative care is developed in South Africa and is available to all citizens. We will not prolong a natural process of dying but we will not in any way actively accelerate dying.
LINK:
The trail will take place next year some time and if the court finding favour of Dieter and Dr Walters that ruling could potentially lead to the decriminalization of assisted dying in South Africa.
V/O:
Assisted dying is legal in a number of countries such as Belgium, the Netherlands, Canada, Colombia and about 8 States in the US.

A positive ruling could also affect the murder case against Prof Davison.
Reginald:
Depending on the circumstance of his case, if those facts in that matter allow him, he could ask for the criminal matter that he is facing to be suspended, pending the outcome of this matter.
V/O:
For Lynne and Dieter who are preparing for the day when Dieter decides to end his life, the application revolves around dignity and the right to have a choice.
Dieter:
I do think it is a very personal question…. I do think strongly that it is a human right to decide.

Meanwhile two more people have applied to the High Court for the right to die at a time they choose – an act that remains illegal in South Africa. Carte Blanche examines the complex and painful decisions around fighting for the right to die. Producer: Eugene Botha Presenter: Derek Watts Script: Dieter Harck: Throughout my life I have enjoyed physical activity… V/O: Dieter Harck suffers from Motor Neuron Disease and gets emotional when he thinks of how much the disease has stolen from him. He used to be a property company director and has adult children and several grandchildren. His partner of 18 years, Lynne Grubb, remembers his endless energy. Lynne: He was extremely active. He was either on his cycle doing a 100 km’s every morning, or at the gym. V/O: But the illness that was diagnosed in 2013 changed all that. Lynne: Dieter is unable to do anything at all for himself. He cannot carry a cup of coffee to his desk. Life for Dieter Harck is a battle. Every day is a battle. V/O: And Dieter knows that in time he will become completely paralysed, and slowly suffocate to death. Dieter: Friends we got to know died, certainly not a death I would wish on anybody. LINK: Dieter has now made the decision that when things become unbearable for him, he wants to end his life with the help of a physician, before the suffering gets too much. V/O: He, together with another terminally ill individual, a Dr Sue Walters who is dying from cancer, have recently launched an action in the Gauteng North High Court to have Assisted Dying legalized. Prof. Willem Landman of Stellenbosch is the co- founder, or an NGO called Dignity South Africa and says there are two kinds of assisted dying. Willem: The one is called physician assisted suicide. A provides the means to B, who self-administers and dies. Physician assisted euthanasia is A supplies and administers to B who the dies as a consequence. 3. LINK: Harck and Dr Walters want to change the law because assisted dying in South Africa is considered illegal and for anybody participating can lead to arrest and a charge of murder. V/O: This is exactly what has happened to Prof Sean Davison of Cape Town, the co-founder of Dignity South Africa. Here he is opening a world conference on assisted dying in Cape Town in September this year. A week after the conference he was arrested and charged with the murder of a very close friend of his, Dr Anrich Burger. Burger once was a medical doctor and very active. In 2005 he was in a car accident in Bostwana, broke his neck and was completely paralysed. Clip: Davison But for Dr Burger, in addition to the undignified life, his body was racked with pain. Now Dr Burger was a medical doctor, he knew all the remedies available to relieve pain. He had tried them all and nothing had worked. For Dr Burger life was miserable. He was desperate to die. V/O: In 2013 he asked Davison to help him to die in a hotel at the Cape Town Waterfront Clip: Davison He asked me to be involved in his death, but he planned it. He was a medical doctor and he wrote the prescription for the medication to end his life. He arranged for a care-giver to take him to the pharmacy to collect the medication. He booked a hotel room at the Waterfront. At the end he wanted me to be there as a friend. Dr Burger committed suicide. V/O: That was 5 years ago, then out of the blue, on the 18 of September Davison, was arrested on a charge of murder and later released on bail. 4. LINK: We asked the NPA why now, after five years, has he been arrested. They sent us a press release, Davison’s affidavit and highlighted the following: “This is not an ordinary murder case and toxicology results are normally a lengthy process. The accused was also not in SA for a period of time. The SAPS was informed that the accused would be entering the RSA hence the arrest.” They also said that “new information obtained suggests that the accused may have committed murder in a similar fashion on more than one occasion”. V/O: Davison is due back in court in November. However, this is not his first brush with the law – in 2010 he was arrested in New Zealand for helping his mother who lived there, to die. He described it in a book and later served 5 months in house arrest after pleading guilty to a charge of assisted suicide. In 2012 he co-founded Dignity South Africa together with Prof Willem Landman. Willem: We founded the NGO with a focus on changing the law. That was our aim. It is still our aim to change the law in South Africa so that people who suffer in a terminal stage of suffering that they can be legitimately and lawfully assisted by qualified people to die in a way that takes away their suffering. V/O: Sheena Swemmer of the Centre for Applied Legal Studies at Wits supports the legal action by Dieter and Dr Sue Walters. She links assisted dying to human rights. Sheena: To be refused the right to choose when to die when in these terminal circumstances is an infringement of one’s right to dignity, one’s right to equality, which together forms the right to autonomy as an individual. Dignified death is part of your right to life. V/O: The current action in the High Court to legalize assisted dying, is not the first of its kind in South Africa. In 2015 terminally ill advocate Robin Stransham-Ford petitioned the Gauteng North High Court to have the right to choose the time and manner of his death. Sheena: So various State Departments opposed the application and it was heard in court, in urgent court. It was presented on the papers, and when we say it was presented on the papers in legal terminology, what we mean is that it is prepared, the entire case is set out on paper, and the judge will decide on that. The judge will not hear any evidence, spoken evidence from experts. V/O: In a landmark ruling Judge Hans Frabricius found in favour of Stransham-Ford, and granted the application. However, the court victory came too late, says Epiphany Stransham-Ford, his daughter. Epihany: It was very bitter-sweet because he had died at 8 o’clock in the morning and the ruling had been passed down only two hours after that. V/O: Epiphany has never questioned or resented her father’s wish to end his life.. He really suffered. Epiphany: Towards the end of his life he could not move, he could not swallow, he could not blink. He was breathing, and his heart was beating but he was not living a life that was worth living. It was his death and I believe he should have been allowed to choose how his end should have come. LINK: Shortly after, various State departments that opposed the Stansham-Ford application, appealed the ruling by the High Court. V/O: The appeal was based on the fact that Stransham-Ford had died before the judgement was handed down and also because in the High Court case there was no thorough interrogation of witnesses because it was an urgent on the papers application. So, the Appeal’s Court rescinded the judgment that assisted dying was legal, based on the technical reasons. However, the Court indicated that it was not unsympathetic towards the merits of the case. Reginald: The Supreme Court of Appeal left a door open for a case to be taken to the High Court again with all the evidence and all the facts. V/O: Reginald Tshabalala is Dieter Harcks’ attorney in the new case and this time round there will a thorough examination of all the evidence through expert witnesses. Derek: The Stransham-Ford case was severely affected when he died. What will happen in either of your clients die? Reginald: The nature of the action that we’ve instituted is so that the action will continue even though they may die in the meantime. V/O: A number of State Departments are opposing the action. This includes the Health professionals Council. Dr Kgosi Letlape is the President of the HPCSA. Letlape: Assisted dying in all is forms, whether it is active or passive, is unlawful in South Africa. It is also unprofessional conduct in terms of our code of ethics. So it is not permissible in the Republic of South Africa. We support proper palliative care, we are in negotiation and the Ministry is leading a path to ensure that palliative care is developed in South Africa and is available to all citizens. We will not prolong a natural process of dying but we will not in any way actively accelerate dying. LINK: The trail will take place next year some time and if the court finding favour of Dieter and Dr Walters that ruling could potentially lead to the decriminalization of assisted dying in South Africa. V/O: Assisted dying is legal in a number of countries such as Belgium, the Netherlands, Canada, Colombia and about 8 States in the US. A positive ruling could also affect the murder case against Prof Davison. Reginald: Depending on the circumstance of his case, if those facts in that matter allow him, he could ask for the criminal matter that he is facing to be suspended, pending the outcome of this matter. V/O: For Lynne and Dieter who are preparing for the day when Dieter decides to end his life, the application revolves around dignity and the right to have a choice. Dieter: I do think it is a very personal question…. I do think strongly that it is a human right to decide.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: In the news: Sean Davison being arrested and accused of murder for helping a friend to die.
metadata.Summary: Prof Sean Davison of Dignity SA was on 18 September arrested for murder for helping a friend, to die. In this insert we explore the issue, the legalities and talk to the main role players in the whole issue around assisted dying.
metadata.Further information: The founder of right-to-die organisation, DignitySA, Sean Davison, has been arrested on a murder charge in Cape Town, a colleague and co-founder confirmed on Wednesday. Davison was arrested on Tuesday, apparently over the death of his friend Anrich Burger in 2013. Burger became a quadriplegic after a car crash.Davison, the professor who helped his mother commit suicide in New Zealand, revealed to News24 in 2014 that he helped Burger end his life. DignitySA co-founder Willem Landman said police executed a search warrant and confiscated Davison's cellphone and laptop.He was kept in Sea Point police station overnight and was due to appear in Cape Town Magistrate's Court on Wednesday. Landman understood that the State wanted R100 000 bail but an amount of R20 000 bail was settled on, which still had to be accepted by a magistrate. Western Cape police spokesperson Lieutenant-Colonel Andre Traut confirmed to News24 that an arrest was made relating to the 2013 death. "This office can confirm that a 57-year-old man was arrested on a charge of murder yesterday relating to an incident in Sea Point on November 2‚ 2013‚ which led to the death of a 43-year-old man. "The suspect is due to make a court appearance in Cape Town today [Wednesday] to face the charge against him."Founder of right-to-die organisation DignitySA, Sean Davison, maintains he has not committed an offence, after making his first appearance in the Cape Town Magistrate's Court on Wednesday for allegedly killing his friend, Anrich Burger. "It is and has always been my contention that I have not committed any offence as alleged in this matter," his lawyer Joshua Greeff read from an affidavit. Davison, 57, was arrested at his home in Pinelands on Tuesday for the 2013 death of Burger, who became a quadriplegic after a car crash. Davison, the professor who helped his mother end her life in New Zealand, revealed to News24 in 2014 that he helped Burger to do the same. Police conducted a search and seizure at his home this week. DignitySA co-founder Willem Landman told News24 Davison's phone and laptop were also confiscated. Prosecutor Megan Blows said the State alleged that the murder was planned or premeditated. She also said "new information has come to light... the accused might have committed other similar offences". It was not immediately clear to which other deaths she was referring. Davison's affidavit in support of his release on bail highlighted an extensive academic career and memberships to numerous professional organisations. He has been a professor of biotechnology at the University of the Western Cape since 2004 and heads up the forensic DNA laboratory there. He helped the Truth and Reconciliation Commission identify the remains of anti-apartheid activists, including the Mamelodi 10 of Pretoria. He also developed a DNA kit to help identify suspects in gang rapes, a service that was offered free to rape victims. In arguing to be released on bail, Davison said he had built an "impeccable reputation" over the years and incarceration could destroy his character and all for which he had worked. He said his three children would not understand his absence because he was an integral part of their lives. As the breadwinner for their family, Davison also feared his wife would not cope financially and emotionally. The court heard that being in custody would jeopardise several projects, outstanding DNA analysis and students under supervision, who Davison assisted. The investigating officer was in possession of his South African and New Zealand passports. Davison pointed out that he abided by all bail conditions while standing trial in New Zealand for helping his cancer-stricken mother end her life. At the time, he pleaded guilty to assisted suicide in the Dunedin High Court and was sentenced to five months' house arrest. He was granted R20 000 bail on Wednesday, which included conditions, such as only leaving the Western Cape with the police's consent and reporting to a police station once a week. On the allegations, Landman said: "The organisation is on record that we stand for changing the law in South Africa to conform with the Constitution and... we do not assist people to die." "What anyone does in their private capacity is their own matter." Davison's arrest has put euthanasia back in the spotlight. In 2015, the North Gauteng High Court in Pretoria ruled that terminally-ill Cape Town advocate Robin Stransham-Ford, 65, had the right to commit suicide with a doctor's help. The following year, the Supreme Court of Appeal found it was wrong for the High Court to issue the order and that it did not fully consider the principles and ambit of changing the common law to encompass consent as a defence to a charge of murder. Stransham-Ford died two hours before the order was granted, as a result of his cancer. Weighing in on Davison's case, defence lawyer William Booth said there had been a number of serious debates in the last decade to change the law on assisted suicide or voluntary euthanasia. "In my opinion, it should be legal under certain circumstances. No legislation has been promulgated where strict criteria is in place," he said. "This is about human dignity. If somebody is going to die... alleviate pain and suffering not only for the patient, but the family too." Davison said in 2012 that many doctors had told him in private that they had helped people to die at their request. "If you don't have a law change, you might be playing Lotto with your doctor." Davison is expected to be back in court on November 16. Since then Archhbishop Emeritus Desmond Tutu has also come out in support of Davison. Treatment: 1. We will follow up on our story of Robin Stransham-Ford who died just before his application to have assisted dying was granted. the ruling was overturned by SCA, but since then two more cases and requests have been lodged. We will speak to his wife and daughter -- Penelope and Epiphany. 2. We will speak to the mother of the person Davison helped to die, and get her perspective -- Wilma Du Pisani 3. In addition we have an exclusive interview with Sean Davison about his mother and how he helped her. We will try and get hold of him, although he has been advised not to speak to the media. 4. We will also speak to Willem Landman, co-founder of Dignity SA. 5. Dr Albertus van Eeden heads up Doctors for Life who are against this. 6. We have also secured an interview with Sally Buitendag, Dognity SA's lawyer. She also represented Stransham-Ford and will represent Davison now. She can speak about all the legal aspects.
